textClass.keywords: primary 62F10 secondary 62M30 Spatial data Measurement error Instrumental variable Three-stage least squares (3SLS)

div.p: In this paper, linear spatial autoregressive (SAR) models with covariate measurement errors are studied. A three-stage least squares (3SLS) estimation method both with Berkson's and classical types of instrumental variables is proposed and asymptotic normality of the proposed estimator using each type of instrumental variables is derived under mild conditions. Simulation studies are conducted to investigate the finite sample performance of the proposed estimator. A real data example is used to illustrate the developed method.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Spatial autoregressive models are popular regression models for spatially distributed data, which take the dependence of the response variable of neighboring units into account. Theories and methods for estimation and inferences based on linear SAR models have been studied extensively in the literature and can be found in the books by Cliff and Ord [11], Anselin [2] and Anselin and Bera [3]. Existing methods mainly include maximum likelihood (ML; see, Ord [28]), generalized two-stage least squares (2SLS; see, Kelejian and Prucha [18]; Lee [20]), method of moments (MM; see, Kelejian and Prucha [19]; Lee [22]) and quasi-maximum likelihood (QML; see Lee [21]). By integrating semiparametric regression techniques, some methods were recently developed for semiparametric SAR models. Among them, Su and Jin [33] proposed the profile quasi-maximum likelihood estimation approach for partially linear SAR models, Su [32] investigated the semiparametric generalized method of moments (GMM) for semiparametric SAR models, and Ai and Zhang [1] and Sun [34]) extended the 2SLS method for partially specified spatial panel data models with fixed-effects and semiparametric varying-coefficient SAR models, respectively. These methods are for the scenario that the variables involved in models can be exactly observed or measured.

It is well known that measurement errors are ubiquitous in practice and statistical modeling that ignores these measurement errors may lead to seriously biased results, especially when measurement errors are contained in observed covariates. There is a large research literature on the classical regression models with measurement errors, for example, Dagenais and Dagenais [13], Reeves et al. [29], Liang et al. [26], Newey [27], Strauss et al. [31], Carroll and Ruppert [8], Gustafson [16], Li and Greene [23], Cui and Li [12], Liang [25], Datta et al. [14], Li and Huang [24] and Zhang et al. [36], among other. Fuller [15] presented a detailed study of linear models with measurement errors, Carroll et al. [9] summarized much of the work for non-linear regression models with measurement errors. Buonaccorsi [6] provided an overview of the main techniques for measurement errors and illustrates their application in more complex mixed and time series models. To the best of our knowledge, there is little literature on the statistical inference of spatial autoregressive models with measurement errors.

Note that measurement error in the dependent variable can be commonly incorporated into the random error term. Most aforementioned methods for SAR models or their extensions still work in SAR models with measurement errors in the dependent variable, while they usually fail in SAR models with measurement errors in covariate variables. For example, it can be proved that the 2SLS estimator is consistent in SAR models with measurement errors in the dependent variable but inconsistent in SAR models with covariate measurement errors. Our simulation results later show that its bias is large and does not reduce as the sample size increases. He and Hu [17] considered the ML and the restricted maximum likelihood (REML) estimators for univariate SAR models with covariate measurement errors. A limitation of these two likelihood-based methods is that they require the ratio of the variances of the measurement error and the model error to be known. In addition, the Likelihood-based methods are not robust under distribution misspecifications. Therefore, it is of great theoretical significance and practical value to develop a robust estimation for SAR models with covariate measurement errors. With this motivation, we consider in this paper the SAR models with covariate measurement errors ⎧ ⎨

Here we assume that measurement errors ξ i , i ∈ {1, . . . , n} are independent and identically distributed and satisfy that E(ξ i |X i , ϵ i ) = 0 and Cov(ξ i |X i , ϵ i ) = Σ ξ , random errors ϵ i , i ∈ {1, . . . , n} are independent and identically distributed with E(ϵ i |X i ) = 0 and Var(ϵ i |X i ) = σ 2 .

Besides the ML-based methods, many estimation methods for regression models with covariate measurement errors can be found in the books by Fuller [15], Carroll et al. [9] and Buonaccorsi [6]. Among them, the moment corrected method and the simulation extrapolation (SIMEX) are two popular methods. However, they suffer from a similar limitation to that of the ML method. The covariance matrix Σ ξ of the measurement error is required to be known or can be estimated from an additional sample of V given X . The instrumental variable method is another general technique for obtaining consistent estimators and has been widely used in practice because it does not need to know or estimate the variance of the measurement error, see, Carter and Fuller [10], Buzas and Stefanski [7], Schennach [30], Gustafson [16], etc. In the literature, there are mainly two types of relationships between the variable X i measured with error and its instrumental variable. One is that X i is the regression function of the instrumental variable (see Fuller [15], Newey [27], Schennach [30]), and the other is that the instrumental variable is the regression function of X i (see Carter and Fuller [10], Carroll et al. [8]). Since these two cases correspond to the Berkson measurement error type and the classical measurement error type of X i , respectively, for convenience, these two types of instrumental variables are referred to as Berkson's type of instrumental variables and the classical type of instrumental variables, respectively.

In this paper, we propose a three-stage least squares estimation method for Model (1) by introducing Berkson's and classical types of instrumental variables, respectively. The proposed estimators are shown to be consistent and asymptotically normally distributed. Simulation results show that the proposed estimation procedure performs well no matter the instrumental variables come from Berkson's type instrumental variables or classical type instrumental variables. The biases and mean square errors of the 3SLS estimators in Model (1) are smaller than those of the 2SLS estimator and decrease quickly as the sample size increases.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 presents the estimation procedure. Section 3 derives the consistency and asymptotic normality of the proposed estimators. Simulation studies are carried out to evaluate the finitesample performance of the proposed estimators in Section 4. A real data example is presented in Section 5. Section 6 is the conclusion. The proofs of the main theorems are relegated to Appendix.

It can be found from Tables 1 and 2 that the proposed 3SLS estimator performs significantly better than the naive 2SLS estimator. The bias of the 3SLS estimator is much smaller than that of the naive 2SLS estimator and decreases quickly as sample size n increases, especially when the measurement error is large (eg., σ 2 ξ 0 = 0.8). As a contrast, the bias of the naive 2SLS estimator changes little and its RMSE hardly decreases as sample size n increases, though its variance is smaller than that of the 3SLS estimator. This shows that the naive 2SLS estimator under Berkson's type of instrumental variables is inconsistent.

On the other hand, we find that different values of π 01 and ρ have little impact on the estimation. When ρ = 0, it implies that Model (11) becomes a classical linear regression model with measurement errors. This implies that the proposed method is robust even if the real model has no spatial dependence. Overall, the results in Tables 1 and 2 show that the proposed 3SLS estimator under Berkson's type of instrumental variables is consistent while the naive 2SLS estimator is inconsistent. Its run-time is just slightly longer than that of the naive 2SLS estimator since one more stage it requires is to project V i onto the space of the instrumental variables and 1 n , which is simple in computation.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: In this paper, by introducing instrumental variables, we proposed a robust estimation method for linear SAS models with covariate measurement errors. The consistency and asymptotical normality are derived for the proposed 3SLS estimators using Berkson's and classical types of the instrumental variables, respectively. The finite sample properties of the 3SLS estimators are investigated through a simulation study. The simulation results show that the proposed estimators perform well under both types of the instrumental variables considered. In comparison with the ML and REML methods of He and Hu [17] for univariate SAR models with covariate measurement errors, the proposed 3SLS method has two advantages: one is that it is a robust distribution-free method, the other is that it can give a consistent estimator without the need to know the ratio of the variances of the measurement error and model error. In practical application, it is usually easier to find the instrumental variable G i than to require an additional sample to estimate the ratio of the variances. For example, a simple selection is to take another surrogate variable of X i as the instrumental variable of V i , while an additional sample often requires additional costs.

In addition, the proposed 3SLS method can be extended to semiparametric SAR models by integrating with semiparametric regression techniques. Further research is warranted to establish a robust estimation method for more flexible SAR models.
